cases.title: A handbook answer carries a grounded citation
cases.prompt: What is a retrieval gate?

trials.reply:
**Retrieval gate**: A cheap check, before any search, of whether this turn needs memory at all.

Most tutorials search memory on every message. The gate asks first: does answering this need what the agent knows about this person? Loopwright can decide by rules (personal words, known names, action verbs) or with one small-model call. Whatever the mode, it fails open: if the decision itself breaks, it retrieves.

Why it exists: Retrieving on every turn is slower, and loosely related memories in the prompt bias the answer. 'What is 2+2' does not need your address.

The tradeoff: A gate that wrongly skips loses a memory the turn needed. So it needs its own eval, and the model keeps a recall tool to pull memory mid-turn when the gate was wrong.

In this repo: `loopwright/memory/gate.py`

[handbook: Retrieval gate]

Related: Push and pull retrieval, Agentic retrieval.

cases.title: A comparison is delegated to parallel workers
cases.prompt: Compare BM25 and embeddings

trials.reply:
Here is how they compare.

**BM25**: Keyword ranking that scores a passage by how often it has the query's words, weighted by how rare they are. It exists because: It is exact. If the user typed 'BILL-4004', BM25 finds the passage with that string, which an embedding may not. Tradeoff: It only matches words. Synonyms, paraphrases and typos score zero. [handbook: BM25]

**embeddings**: Text turned into vectors so that similar meaning lands close together. It exists because: Keyword search misses paraphrase: 'booking' does not match 'schedule'. Vector search finds passages that mean the same thing in different words. Tradeoff: Dense search is weak on exact tokens such as error codes, ids and names, and it always returns its nearest neighbours even when nothing is relevant, so it needs a similarity floor. [handbook: Embeddings]

cases.title: The critic sends a comparison back for a bottom line
cases.prompt: Compare the retrieval gate and compaction

trials.reply:
Here is how they compare.

**retrieval gate**: A cheap check, before any search, of whether this turn needs memory at all. It exists because: Retrieving on every turn is slower, and loosely related memories in the prompt bias the answer. 'What is 2+2' does not need your address. Tradeoff: a gate that wrongly skips loses a memory the turn needed. So it needs its own eval, and the model keeps a recall tool to pull memory mid-turn when the gate was wrong. [handbook: Retrieval gate]

**compaction**: Replacing older conversation with a summary when history outgrows its share of the window. It exists because: Without it a long session either overflows the window or spends most of every call re-reading old small talk. Tradeoff: It is lossy and irreversible in the model's view: whatever the summary omits is gone. That is why durable facts are also written to long-term memory, and why the recent messages stay verbatim. [handbook: Compaction]

In short: A cheap check, before any search, of whether this turn needs memory at all. Replacing older conversation with a summary when history outgrows its share of the window.

cases.title: A web question goes to web_search and the answer cites URLs
cases.prompt: Search the web for agent evaluation best practices

trials.reply:
I searched the web for "agent evaluation best practices" (demo). The top results:
1. **A practical guide to evaluating AI agents**: Start an agent evaluation suite with twenty to fifty realistic cases drawn from real usage and known failures. Prefer deterministic graders that check outcomes and tool calls, and add a model judge only for criteria code cannot check. (demo://agent-evals-guide)
2. **Field notes: what prompt caching saved us**: After moving static instructions and tool definitions to the front of the prompt and keeping tool order stable, our cache hit rate on agent loops rose sharply and input cost per turn fell by more than half. The main lesson was that a timestamp near the top of the system prompt had been invalidating the cache on every call. (demo://prompt-caching-notes)
3. **Model Context Protocol in one page**: The Model Context Protocol standardises how AI applications connect to tools and data. A server exposes tools over JSON-RPC; any client can discover and call them. (demo://mcp-overview)
